title: What Do We Teach When Nobody Knows?
author: What Teachers Have to Say Source: whatteachershavetosay.substack.com
summary: A careful survey of three economist camps on AI's labor market effects leads to a clear pedagogical conclusion: because nobody actually knows which scenario will unfold, transferable skills are the only hedge that works across all futures. The Alarmed (Korinek, Amodei) believe major white-collar displacement will arrive within a decade and cite a Stanford pre-print showing a 16% relative employment decline for early-career workers in AI-exposed occupations since ChatGPT launched. The Patient (Narayanan, Acemoglu) argue the timeline is measured in decades, pointing to organizational friction, hallucination-driven productivity gaps, and historical analogies (electricity took 40 years to reshape factory floors). The Excited (Autor, Andreessen) focus on what gets built rather than what disappears. Yale Budget Lab data through April 2026 shows macro employment stability even as the occupational mix shifts faster than past tech transitions. For educators, the author argues that content knowledge is exactly what domain-specific AI disruption threatens most; transferable skills — analytical thinking, adaptability, relational intelligence — are the hedge. The disruption of 'expert-novice bonds' is also flagged: if AI handles entry-level cognitive work, junior workers never build the judgment that entry-level tasks historically transmitted.
points: Three serious economist camps (Alarmed, Patient, Excited) have examined the same evidence on AI's labor-market effects and reached genuinely different conclusions — the honest position is radical uncertainty about timeline, magnitude, and outcome.

Yale Budget Lab data through April 2026 shows macro employment stability, but early-career workers in the most AI-exposed occupations have already seen a 16% relative employment decline since ChatGPT's launch in late 2022.

Content knowledge is the most vulnerable to domain-specific AI disruption; transferable skills — analytical thinking, source evaluation, adaptability, relational intelligence — are the hedge that works across all three scenarios.

If AI handles entry-level cognitive work, junior workers never develop the judgment that entry-level tasks historically transmitted, disrupting 'expert-novice bonds' and the generational propagation of expertise.
The author's working thesis: disruption will arrive in 'staggered waves, task by task, domain by domain' — cumulative and retrospectively obvious, but difficult to see while it is happening.
quotes: The debate is live, contested among credentialed people who have looked carefully at the same evidence and come to genuinely different conclusions.

Content knowledge is domain-specific, and as such, exactly what's most vulnerable to domain-specific waves of disruption. That's why I'm so passionate about transferable skills being the hedge that works across all three futures.

A student who can think analytically, evaluate the reliability of a source or a system, adapt to novel problems, and work effectively with other humans is positioned for the world the Excited describe and resilient enough for the world the Alarmed fear.

If AI handles entry-level cognitive work, new workers never build the judgment that entry-level work historically transmitted. You can't supervise and evaluate AI outputs at a senior level if you never developed the reasoning capacity to do the work yourself as a junior.

I think it will happen in staggered waves, task by task, domain by domain, as specific AI capabilities mature and reach specific sectors... What I don't believe we'll find is a single moment of disruption.
